b: I'm an AI sceptic, but not in the sense that I don't think it's occasionally useful. I just don't think the people who are making it are the sort of people who should have any control of it at all. I've been working with it and studying it for about three years now, and it's honestly great for some things. I'm using it to write the code for a small mobile game I've had in mind for over a decade but just haven't been able to get good enough or fast enough at coding to make it worthwhile. I would never, ever, trust it to do anything that was important, it that I didn't know enough to check its work.

The way LLMs are built requires that they have a random factor thrown into their workflow. This is referred to as the “heat” of the process. That randomness is what allows them to be flexible enough to chat. It also means they'll answer differently each time you ask the same thing. Most of the time, that difference will be wording, or something else irrelevant, but sometimes, they'll just be wrong. This is party of how they work. With current technology, it's unavoidable. There's ways to mitigate the wrong, Steer them toward the right answer, restrict the wrong or harmful answers…. But they can't avoid it completely without losing the ability to improvise like they do. It's referred to as deterministic or non-deterministic. As part of that, you can never predict where or how much they'll be wrong, but it will always be some, and sometimes a while lot.

The other big risk for AI is “cognitive offloading”. As humans our brains and bodies only stay good at what we do a lot. Use it or lose it. Stop biking to work and drive everywhere, your aerobic abilities decline. Use Google Maps to get everywhere, and you're sense of direction gets shakier. Rely on AI to write all your emails and do all your think, and u b dumer fast.

So, I'm in favor of using it to cut through crap, like the sorts of things a human resources department wants you to do, or to amplify a weaker skill you have, like coding things that are fun but unimportant. But didn't let them do anything that's important to you, or take over a skill that you don't want to lose. Cory Doctorow refers to it as the centaur vs. reverse centaur. A centaur is a human brain and hands, with the speed and power of a horse. A reverse centaur is an idiot horse controlling the weak body of a human. Some do AI determined scutwork, some let AI set the pace or priorities. So let them speed up audio transcription, but check it. So let them out your receipts in chronological order, or even categorize them by purchase type. But check it.
